title: At-most-once vs at-least-once delivery
description: Learn the difference between at-most-once and at-least-once message delivery semantics. Understand the trade-offs and when to use each.

data.text: Message delivery semantics define the guarantees a messaging system provides about whether and how many times a message is delivered. Understanding these guarantees is crucial for building reliable distributed systems.
At-most-once delivery means each message is delivered zero or one times, but never more than once. Messages may be lost but never duplicated.

items: Fire-and-forget—sender doesn't wait for acknowledgment
No retry logic—messages lost on failure
Lowest latency—no coordination overhead
Simplest implementation
Accepts data loss for performance

data.title: When to Use
data.text: Metrics, logging, non-critical telemetry, real-time data where freshness matters more than completeness, scenarios where occasional loss is acceptable.
At-least-once delivery means each message is delivered one or more times. Messages are never lost but may be duplicated.

items: Ack/retry—sender retries until acknowledgment received
No data loss—messages eventually delivered
Potential duplicates—same message delivered multiple times
Requires idempotency handling
Higher latency due to retries

data.title: When to Use
data.text: Critical business events, financial transactions, user notifications, any scenario where data loss is unacceptable and you can handle duplicates.
True exactly-once delivery is impossible in distributed systems. What systems call "exactly-once" is usually at-least-once delivery with idempotent processing.

items: Network failures make true exactly-once impossible
Exactly-once semantics require end-to-end idempotency
Kafka's "exactly-once" = idempotent producer + transactional consumer
Most systems implement exactly-once via deduplication
Don't rely on messaging layer alone for exactly-once

data.title: Critical Insight
data.text: If you need exactly-once semantics, implement idempotency in your consumers. Make duplicate processing safe rather than trying to prevent duplicates at the network level.

items.title: At-Most-Once
items.description: Pros: Fast, simple, low overhead. Cons: Data loss possible, no guarantees. Use for telemetry, metrics, non-critical data.

items.title: At-Least-Once
items.description: Pros: No data loss, reliable. Cons: Duplicates possible, requires idempotency, higher latency. Use for critical events.

data.text: When using at-least-once delivery, you must handle potential duplicates idempotently.

items: Unique IDs—use message IDs to detect duplicates
Deduplication tables—track processed message IDs
Conditional writes—use database constraints
Idempotent operations—make duplicates safe (e.g., SET value = X)
Natural idempotency—some operations are inherently idempotent

data.text: Consider the cost of data loss versus the cost of handling duplicates.

items: At-most-once: When speed matters more than completeness, when losing data is acceptable
At-least-once: When data loss is unacceptable, when you can implement idempotency
Consider your consumers' ability to handle duplicates
Factor in the complexity of idempotency implementation
Evaluate the impact of retries on system load
